It's an excellent game with a beautiful world to explore, tons of creative characters, a variety of weapons, and a very well done combat system. This is my first souls-like game, and it's got me interested in playing some more from the genre.

The first hour I put into the game, I completely misunderstood the premise, and I was very frustrated at it - as soon as I left the starting area, I tried battling the high-level horseback rider, and felt like I had to defeat it to progress. Learning that some enemies can (and should) just be sprinted past was helpful. I had a friend who kind of guided the beginning of the game for me, but if I hadn't had that, I think I would have needed a tutorial or many wiki pages to figure out where to go and what to do. The amount of freedom the game offers can be overwhelming at first, and it's easy to miss key moments, items, or concepts entirely.

The early game offers a really rewarding cycle of finding new weapons, getting a spike in power, being able to fight your way through new areas, which in turn offer new weapons, and so on. It also feels very well paced in that you naturally encounter a lot of NPC's, points of interest, and discover new areas of the map quickly enough to maintain interest, but not so quickly that you feel like you're missing a lot of action. It felt like Limgrave had the most amount of effort put into it by a long shot.

The mid game really let Elden Ring shine - I was progressing questlines, fighting tons of optional bosses, upgrading my favorite weapons, and exploring cool places like the capitol city, the academy of raya lucaria, the underground world. Fights felt intense, but fair, I had a general direction to go but felt free to explore the entirety of the game, I had a really good time at this point in the game.

The late game to Elden Ring feels very rushed - the final unlockable map areas felt very empty compared to the rest of the game (especially mountaintops of the giants) and had considerably fewer characters or quests (at least, that I ran into). All the optional bosses I had done before had made my character strong enough that now the main quest bosses felt less challenging, almost to the point of being disappointing. At this point, I also found I was running into copies of bosses I had already defeated, mainly by doing the dungeons ahead of time. It sort of weakened the impact of seeing them appear later on. Finishing NPC quests was difficult at this point, as various things you can do accidentally throughout the game can affect where you are at in your questline, or where NPCs spawn, or even whether they are alive or dead, so much of the late game before the final boss revolved around keeping 10 wiki tabs open and trying to figure between tons of fast traveling where NPC's might be, or whether their quest was impossible to finish at this point. Suddenly the "life" of the map felt like it had receded into the background, and it was more like a big empty expanse. Not that it was bad at this point, or that this part made the game as whole bad, but it felt like the developers had put 80% of their time into the early game and then really flown through the final 10 hours worth of content. 

The highlights of the game, for me, were those early moments of exploration in this big, beautiful world - the first 30 or 40 hours of this game just feel so cool, building your character up and getting stronger and stronger, and feeling bolder to go into harder areas, but not so strong that you can just blow through them. Really, really cool experience. The fight against Malenia and the final boss of the game were also absolutely fantastic - brutally difficult, but consistent and fair. They felt so impossible and punishing on the first attempt, and by the final attempt, they felt like a dance. Very well designed.

Overall I would give this game an 8.5/10, it's a very strong game that feels a little unnecessarily bloated at times, but gives you the freedom to avoid that bloat, and enough variety to still enjoy it otherwise. I would highly recommend this game to anyone interested in the souls-like genre.

Open World with Classic Souls Appeal

Pros:

-Absolutely beautiful locations with incredible scenic vistas. I find myself constantly taking screenshots. Hidden pathways and secrets scattered throughout. The map system encourages exploration - pick up an area map in game and it'll show you the surrounding landmarks (without divulging their names or other details), which you can then check out for yourself. 

-Some of the coolest cutscenes in any game ever. Don't skip any of them unless you've already watched it.

-Amazing soundtrack all around.

-Minimalist HUD that doesn't hold your hand or take away from the beautiful visuals.

-Intricate lore subtly conveyed through architecture, item descriptions, and limited NPC dialogue. Highly open to interpretation.

-The gameplay is challenging if you want it to be, or easy if you want it to be. This might be the most flexible of all the souls games in terms of gameplay and difficulty. If you want it difficult, play solo, use a melee build, forego spirit ash summons, spells and ranged weapons. If you're struggling, you can summon your friends or spirit ash NPCs to help you. 

The open world is also your friend here: you can skip ahead of some bosses, or level up or grab new weapons and fight them later. If you want to use a different build - let's say you're a warrior and you want to try magic instead - you can completely change stats without needing to start over. Other games might use a difficulty setting to alter enemies' health and damage, but not Elden Ring - the variety of mechanics and playstyles are the difficulty slider. 

-The new movement mechanics make the gameplay more varied and interesting. There are jump and crouch buttons, so you're no longer limited to the usual combat roll and sprint for dodging attacks - you can duck and jump them too. The jump attack is quite powerful, and the crouch allows you to sneak effectively past enemies or get backstabs.

-The bosses are challenging, especially the ones in the endgame, especially for melee builds. Expect to constantly dodge and look for the perfect opening, but don't overdo it - the bosses have attack timings designed to trip you up if you panic roll or heal at the wrong time.

Cons: 

-The lock-on camera is still garbage and it will spaz out on you when enemies jump around, leaving you confused.

-The net code for multiplayer seems to be poor. If you participate in an invasion or arena combat expect to see lag. It can even become game-breaking. The devs need to fix this issue if they're going to keep adding multiplayer.

-NPC quests can become confusing. You might need to read the wiki to determine an NPC's location or whether you've locked yourself out of their questline. They change locations constantly and frequently don't tell you where they're going. 

-Many reused assets. Many cookie-cutter enemies that slightly differ in color or attack pattern. Not all areas of the game are interesting either, particularly toward the endgame. I wonder if time constraints played a role here.

-The final boss is somewhat unimpressive.

-The open world flexibility can ruin bosses or areas if you skip them or simply don't notice them, then level up your character and come back to them later. If your stats are "too high" for a particular area then you will shred everything in it with minimal effort. This can be disappointing for players who want a challenge, which is the main appeal of souls-type games.

Conclusion:
Elden Ring has its flaws but it's a solid first open world game for FromSoft.

**Review of "Elden Ring": An Unforgettable Journey into a Vast, Enigmatic World**

As someone who has never ventured into the realm of "souls-like" games, I approached "Elden Ring" with a mix of apprehension and excitement. The hype surrounding it was palpable; from dazzling trailers to glowing reviews, it seemed that everyone was enamored with this masterpiece. I finally decided to take the plunge, and what an exhilarating ride it turned out to be! If you're contemplating purchasing this game, allow me to share my overwhelmingly positive experience and hopefully entice you to dive into this extraordinary adventure.

**A Visual Feast for the Senses**

From the moment I first stepped foot into the world of the Lands Between, I was utterly mesmerized by the game’s stunning visuals. "Elden Ring" boasts an artistic direction that seamlessly blends dark fantasy with lush open environments. The sprawling landscapes are meticulously crafted, each area distinct yet interconnected in ways that evoke curiosity and awe. Whether I was traversing vast fields dotted with wildflowers or navigating the intricacies of ancient ruins, every corner I turned unveiled breathtaking vistas that felt alive. Day and night cycles, weather changes, and the ethereal glow of distant landmarks added layers of immersion, making exploration not just a necessity but a joy!

**An Engaging Narrative That Captivates**

What struck me most about "Elden Ring" is its compelling narrative. It's clear that the minds behind the game—most notably Hidetaka Miyazaki and George R.R. Martin—brought an epic quality to the storytelling. The lore is rich and immersive, woven into the environment, character dialogues, and even item descriptions. As I encountered various beings in my journey—each with their own background and motivations—I was drawn deeper into an intricate tale of ambition, betrayal, and the search for power. The way the story unfolds is not reliant on traditional cutscenes; instead, it’s organically revealed through exploration and interaction, rewarding those curious enough to piece together the fragments of this grand saga.

**Gameplay that Exhilarates and Challenges**

Now, let’s talk about gameplay. Initially, I was intimidated by the reputation these types of games have for being brutally difficult. However, I found that "Elden Ring" presents a balanced challenge that, while demanding, never feels insurmountable. The combat mechanics are fluid and satisfyingly responsive, allowing for a range of play styles. Whether you favor a swift, agile approach or a more defensive, tank-like strategy, there’s room to mold your character to your liking.

What truly captivated me is the level of freedom "Elden Ring" affords players. I could venture down different paths, tackle challenges in any order, and indeed embrace failure as a learning curve rather than a roadblock. There’s something magical about stumbling upon a hidden dungeon or secret boss in the wilderness—every corner you explore feels rewarding.

**Customization: Your Adventure, Your Way**

In addition to the rich landscapes and thrilling encounters, "Elden Ring" offers an extensive character customization system. As I crafted my avatar, I was amazed at the variety of options available. From different classes and skill sets to a plethora of weapons and spells, the ability to personalize my adventure turned my character into a unique reflection of my play style. Choosing how to face the myriad of foes and obstacles was thrilling, and every choice felt significant.

**Multiplayer Elements that Enhance the Experience**

One of the charming aspects of "Elden Ring" is its multiplayer component. As a newcomer, I appreciated the ability to summon other players for assistance during challenging segments. This cooperative gameplay option not only provided support during difficult encounters but also fostered a sense of camaraderie in an otherwise solitary experience. In addition, the Ghost Summons mechanic allowed for moments of teamwork that made even the toughest bosses feel achievable. Sharing these victories with others heightened the overall enjoyment.

**An Unforgettable Atmosphere**

The atmosphere of "Elden Ring" deserves special mention. There’s a haunting quality to the sound design that perfectly complements the visuals. The score is sweeping and epic, perfectly capturing the essence of exploration and confrontation. Each sound—be it the rustling of leaves, the approach of a fearsome enemy, or the delicate plucking of strings during emotional moments—immersed me fully in this fantastical world. It’s a sensory experience that lingered long after I stepped away from my console.

**A Testament to Craftsmanship**

Ultimately, "Elden Ring" is more than just a game; it’s an experience—a testament to the power of video gaming as an art form. The meticulous attention to detail, the robust mechanics, and the profound storytelling come together to create a piece that transcends mere entertainment. For those of you considering this journey, prepare to lose yourself in a world that feels both hauntingly beautiful and alive. After my time with "Elden Ring," I found not just a game but an entire universe filled with memories, triumphs, and a deep sense of wonder.

In conclusion, if you’re someone who is intrigued by adventure, captivated by storytelling, and excited to explore vast, mysterious worlds, "Elden Ring" is a must-have. Even as a newcomer, I can wholeheartedly say that this game has set a new standard for my gaming experiences. Don't just take my word for it; embark on this incredible journey yourself—you won’t regret it!

This level of freedom in how you develop and play your character ensures that every player’s experience is unique and deeply satisfying.

The artistry in Elden Ring extends beyond its visual and auditory presentation. The soundtrack is a powerful and evocative accompaniment to the journey, enhancing the emotional impact of every moment. The hauntingly beautiful score perfectly complements the game’s atmosphere, drawing you deeper into its mystical world.

Elden Ring isn’t just a game; it’s an experience that redefines what’s possible in the open-world RPG genre. It is a masterwork of design, storytelling, and innovation that will be remembered and celebrated for years to come. Whether you’re a seasoned fan of FromSoftware’s games or new to their world, Elden Ring offers an unforgettable journey that is nothing short of transcendent. Half of the game is fun. Once you get to the snow region, it becomes a massive slog. The hype was way too high, but it's worth the price when it's on sale. The story is interesting as always.

 The "difficulty" everyone champions is mostly stuff targeted at preventing you from being allowed to control your character. Tons of stunlock, enemies perfectly dodging 100% of projectiles, massive combos, attacks timed to hit you again if you try to roll out of those combos, and many enemies simply never stop for an opening. Everything also hits extremely hard; even a full tank build doesn't usually last very long.

Many bosses are reused repeatedly, often by just adding more of them to the fight. 

Some bosses are very good, but ruined by one particular design choice. for example: One boss somewhat slower, powerful attacks, with mid sized AOE, but their timings are all very strange, which makes it a fun fight. Unfortunately, for the first half of that fight, they start with two very tough enemies alongside them, and their weapon has the ability to buff nearby allies, effectively turning both of them into minibosses that you have to fight 3 on 1 in a small arena.

Open world tends to mean [i]empty[/i] world, and Elden Ring is not an exception, huge swaths of the map have nothing in them. There's an entire endgame area that's almost completely empty, and you'll want to rush through it because visibility there is nil. The limitations of linear/ semi linear worlds mean more care and planning is put into them than open worlds.

Many quests fail unless you do every step at very specific times, so you have to make sure you don't do any progress before all those steps are done.

Lastly, for much of the later game equipment, you'd be better off cheating it in on a fresh file than doing new game plus, if you wish to play with it. Stats cap at 99, and NG+ doesn't change this, it just makes all the enemies harder. After 1 playthough you'll already be close to capping your main stats, so you wont be able to progress at all after a bit.

This game is [i]FAR[/i] from perfect, and any criticism is often met with a simple, unhelpful "git gud" by the community. That said, there's is a lot of fun to be had here, especially in the first half.

I’ve played for over 273 hours and I’m done with this game.  I kept playing hoping the gameplay would get better.  If you enjoy taking death after death, then you will love this game.  I would take so many deaths defeating an area or dungeon boss that it would feel more like an exercise in frustration than it would a great accomplishment.  More often than not, the item rewards were hardly worth the effort.
There are a lot of areas in the game where you have to make jumps from one ledge or one building to another.  I took countless deaths attempting these and losing whatever progress I’d made in the game.  Some of them would have an enemy shooting or throwing projectiles at you while trying to make these jumps or navigating narrow paths and knocking you to your death.  As if I wasn’t struggling enough with the thousands of deaths I was taking killing my way through the game.  This part of the gameplay is completely unnecessary.
There are multiple questlines in this game, but they are impossible to follow since there is no quest log.  I’m not asking for the open world map to be littered with quest markers, but it would be nice to be able to at least review what the last NPC told you so you could pick up where you left off.  
There are several dungeons, underground areas and castles where I found myself running around in circles.  A couple of people I know wanted to group up and play together, but it’s extremely difficult to do.  All in all, I wanted a game that would be worth playing through multiple times to try out different character builds.  I didn’t even finish my initial playthrough because of the ridiculous number of deaths and the amount of frustration with the game.  I can’t imagine wanting to subject myself to another horrible playthrough.  I will never buy another game from this company or recommend this game to anyone.

I was really excited to play Elden Ring, but unfortunately, I could not get my official Xbox controller to work, despite the game claiming to have controller support. Here’s everything I tried to fix the issue, but nothing worked:

1. Checked the controller settings in Steam - Made sure that "Xbox Configuration Support" and "Generic Gamepad Configuration Support" were enabled in the Steam controller settings.


2. Restarted Steam and the game - Tried launching Elden Ring multiple times, both with and without Big Picture mode, but still no luck.


3. Tried a different USB port - Switched my controller to every USB port available, thinking it might be a hardware connection issue, but no response from the game.


4. Updated my controller drivers - Downloaded the latest drivers for my Xbox controller from the official Microsoft website, but this didn’t resolve the issue.


5. Tested the controller with other games - My controller worked flawlessly with other Steam games, proving the problem is specifically with Elden Ring.


6. Disabled Steam Input for Elden Ring - Went into the game’s properties in my library and turned off the Steam Input to see if that would fix it, but still no response.


7. Checked in-game settings - Made sure the controller was selected as the primary input device in Elden Ring’s settings, but it simply didn’t recognize it.


8. Verified the game files - Used the “Verify Integrity of Game Files” option in Steam to ensure no corrupt files were causing the problem, but this didn’t help.


9. Disabled any overlays - Turned off any overlays like Steam Overlay, Xbox Game Bar, and even GeForce Experience, thinking they might be interfering, but it didn’t change anything.


10. Reinstalled the game - I even went as far as completely uninstalling and reinstalling Elden Ring, but that was just another wasted effort.



Despite all these troubleshooting steps, I couldn’t get my Xbox controller to work with Elden Ring. It’s incredibly frustrating, especially since the game advertises full controller support. I can't recommend this game if you plan on playing with a controller. It's a shame, as I was really looking forward to experiencing this title. Hopefully, FromSoftware fixes this issue soon, but until then, I’d advise controller users to be cautious before purchasing.

Elden Ring is like willingly stepping into a battlefield where the only guarantee is pain, but the kind of pain that leaves you craving more. It’s Dark Souls on steroids—only this time, the world is so massive, you can get lost in it for hours, just to stumble upon something even more soul-crushing than the last boss that wrecked you. And you’ll love every second of it.

The combat? Oh, it’s brutal. Every enemy looks like it crawled straight out of a nightmare, designed to make sure you second-guess every decision you’ve ever made. But when you finally land that perfect parry or take down that seemingly impossible boss, it’s like a rush of adrenaline straight to your veins. You’ve earned that win, and no one can take it from you. But don’t get cocky, because this game lives to humble you. Every. Single. Time.

The world? A sprawling fever dream of chaos, beauty, and terror all rolled into one. You can’t explore for more than five minutes without being ambushed by something monstrous, and yet you’ll keep pushing forward, eyes wide, because the environment just dares you to see what’s around the next corner. And trust me, it’s usually something that wants to rip your face off.

The story? Classic FromSoftware—vague and scattered across cryptic lore, but somehow dripping with dark allure. You’ll spend hours piecing it together, and even when you think you’ve got it, the game leaves you with more questions than answers. But honestly, the story isn’t what keeps you coming back. It’s the challenge. It’s the thrill of dying 30 times in the same spot, only to finally crack the code and make that zone your kingdom.

The open world is your playground, and by playground, I mean death trap. There are no hand-holds here—no map markers to coddle you, no easy routes. You explore at your own risk, and most of the time, you’ll pay for that curiosity with your life. But that’s the beauty of Elden Ring. It doesn’t care about your feelings. It wants you to fight, to suffer, to overcome.

Is it frustrating? Hell yes. Is it worth every moment of that frustration? Absolutely. Elden Ring will drag you through the mud, but by the end, you’ll feel like you conquered the impossible. You’ll wear every scar from this game with pride, and that’s why it’s a masterpiece. It doesn’t just test your skills—it tests your will. And if you survive, you’ll walk away feeling like a god.

Elden Ring stands out as an extraordinary achievement in game design, particularly for its impressive customization options and exhilarating gameplay. From the moment you enter the Lands Between, you’re greeted with a level of freedom that lets you tailor your experience like never before.

The character customization is simply amazing. You can shape not just your character’s appearance but also how you approach the game. Whether you want to be a stealthy rogue, a mighty sorcerer, or a heavily armored tank, the choices are extensive. The variety of weapons, spells, and gear allows for countless combinations, ensuring that every player can find a build that suits their style. This level of personalization makes each playthrough feel unique and rewarding.

The gameplay itself is brutally fun, combining a sense of challenge with a rewarding flow. While it may be the most accessible game FromSoftware has released, don’t be fooled into thinking it’s easy. Each encounter demands skill and strategy, with the satisfying thrill of mastering tough bosses and overcoming obstacles. The weighty, impactful combat makes every victory feel earned, and the adrenaline rush keeps you coming back for more.

However, the multiplayer aspect leaves something to be desired. While teaming up with friends is a great concept, the execution can be frustrating. Connection issues and limitations in summoning can interrupt the experience, making it feel less seamless than it should be. This aspect can be a letdown, especially when you’re eager to share the adventure with others.

In summary, Elden Ring is a 10/10 experience that brilliantly combines deep customization with brutally enjoyable gameplay. The world is expansive and filled with secrets, encouraging exploration and discovery. Despite some co-op frustrations, the game is an absolute must-play for anyone looking for an unforgettable adventure. FromSoftware has crafted another classic, and it’s a journey you won’t want to miss.

I give it 9/10.

Positives: game of the decade, you already know this is a masterpiece. I really loved the exploring, bosses, leveling up and growing stronger in early, mid, and late game (till you reach areas like consecrated snowfield and haligtree). Endgame bosses are also awesome, with the right build they are a fair, fun, and rewarding fight. The lore is quite epic too.

Negatives:

1. Some dungeons have incredibly frustrating mechanics. These are optional dungeons, so it's not too much of a negative.

2. NPC quests - very hard to progress some of these quests without looking up a guide, because the NPCs often don't tell you where they are going next, and they could go to an area you have already explored. And if you do another NPC quest or story progression, you might end up breaking an ongoing NPC quest and be permanently locked out from completing it, so there is a very specific order to completing some of these quests.

3. Exploring endgame areas and dungeons is incredibly frustrating. Early and mid game bosses now appear as regular enemies. Both damage and health of regular enemies are scaled very high, and annoying enemies group together. Each level up takes way more runes so it is very likely to lose all progress while exploring blind.

4. Not all builds are equally viable in endgame. Some of the very hard endgame bosses (eg Malenia) become much simpler with the right build, but a lot of fun builds are not very viable.

So overall it's a decent game with good and fun combat and that's the biggest and perhaps only good aspect of it. It's like a hack-n-slash diablo-type game but harder (minus) and played from third person perspective (plus). So as you'd expect, it's very grindy and loot based - not as much as hack-n-slash games though. Timing your attacks and your defenses is more important here, but your gear, equipment can totally change your playstyle and how you approach enemies. The typical hack-n-slash game stuff.

Lots of comments have been made about its difficulty. It's generally hard, but it's not really that hard, especially if you ride the horse. The combat is skillful and intelligent and takes some getting used to. Again, combat is by far the best part of the game, hence my positive rating.
Melee combat is much more fun and fleshed out than ranged.
Huge variety of enemies, creatures, bosses - not that this is necessarily good, but it keeps things fresh.
I really liked the difficulty of AI invaders, they present a real challenge and it's the most fun combat I've had so far, much more fun that bosses.

There are some more advanced techniques that go much more in depth to give you an edge, but to really take advantage of them you need to grind... Good luck with that.

PvP/PvE, generally the multiplayer side, is much worse than I expected. It's just there.. and it's quite limited.
I spawned coop buddies once to defeat a boss, one of them was so overlevelled he killed the boss in 3 hits. It's hard to find someone at your level to play. Another time, I spawned a couple of coop buddies to clear a dungeon and then another one comes and harasses the entire team trying to kill us all. Multiplayer is boring, single player is definitely more fun. Or perhaps multiplayer with only players you know, if that's possible, that could be viable too.

Now, other than that, it has no story, no characters, no real quests, no music - aside from one decent track.
The game is totally aimless, you roam around the land and kill monsters, just like diablo-clones. Don't get fooled to think that this makes it an "open world" game, the way we know open world.

At this point, I'm bored of the game because it's just too repetitive. The combat is fun so I could see myself coming back occasionally playing some short sessions but that's it.

Not bad, definitely not great.

Elden Ring is a game of extremes. The world and the lore of the Lands Between are astounding in their scope and beauty. The world map is expansive, and the locations within it are, in many instances, jaw dropping. The game's story takes a back seat to the very act of exploration, serving often as a simple means of guiding the player in the correct direction.
 
The combat is tense, snappy, and fun. dodge rolls, heavy attacks, light attacks parries, melee, range, spells, buffs, debuffs. Combat has so many fun decision making points in every encounter and generally feels good.

The leveling system is deceptively simple. There are main attributes that govern damage and other player stats. these should be pumped while allowing a minimum amount of points for health, mana, and stamina, and then pouring remaining points into whatever is required to make the build work.

All of these are excellent systems and they work together to make Elden Ring a joy to experience. However they're held back by glaring oversights and poor design decisions. 

That large map feels dead to the player. There are almost no friendly NPCs. There are no cities, no towns, no trading hubs. There is only an unending amount of nightmarish monsters who aim to kill you over and over again. The lore is buried under so many discover-able items that it's easy to miss major plot points. At one point the penultimate boss will say "from this point forward, I fight as Horah Loux!" I have no clue who this is. I was never told and I missed the inscription on some ring in some chest in some cave, somewhere. likewise the quest system is, for lack of a better word, a disaster. Having to initiate conversations with the same person multiple times before they disappear to reappear somewhere else on the massive game map is ridiculous.

The combat is wonderful fun against other enemies that are roughly the same size as your character. against a vast number of enemies that are both fast and multiple stories tall, the immersion of dodge rolling through a minivan sized sword is nonexistent, and the lock on camera cannot keep up. 

The game has no concept of balance between fights either. I was able to crush the above mentioned penultimate boss into the ground inside of 10 seconds. the final boss was immune to bleed, which I had based my build around. Every decision I had made up until that point ceased to matter for this boss. My bleed talisman? useless. my bleed helm? useless. My 80 points in arcane? a direct hindrance. Perhaps I should respec my build but...

items need to be leveled using a finite resource found randomly throughout the map. swapping a build inherently requires you to level another item. this means that items found later in the game are almost impossible to use if you've not been stingey with your leveling items.

and that end of the game takes forever to arrive. the game loses steam at around the 50 hour mark, then continues for another 20-30 hours.


Does this mean Elden Ring is bad? No. in many ways it's remarkable. a towering achievement of world design. but it's held back from greatness by some truly ridiculous balance decisions. I can still strongly recommend it, but expect some frustrations that should have been addressed prior to release.

Elden Ring is an astonishing experience that, without a doubt, has become one of the most impactful games I've ever played. It has likely surpassed some of my all-time favorites, carving out a permanent place in my gaming memories. It's rare for a game to leave such a deep impression, but Elden Ring accomplished just that—I genuinely enjoyed every moment of it.

Graphics:
While not the most graphically advanced title, Elden Ring still manages to impress and is visually stunning through and through. Its graphical fidelity might not push the envelope, but it looks superb nonetheless, particularly due to one crucial aspect: its art direction.

Design and Art Direction:
This is where Elden Ring truly shines. The art and design are nothing short of exceptional, with every landscape, creature, and ruin meticulously crafted. You can see the immense thought, passion, and effort poured into every corner of the world. It’s not surprising, given it’s a FromSoftware game, but the sheer attention to detail and the atmospheric beauty still left me in awe.

Lore and Worldbuilding:
The worldbuilding is equally masterful, although I do have some reservations about its approach. The lore is deep and intricately woven, but it’s also quite elusive. It follows the classic FromSoftware method—offering minimal exposition and requiring players to read item descriptions, piece together clues, and make connections on their own. While I appreciate the layers and complexity, there were times I found myself struggling to grasp what was happening or even what my immediate goal was, aside from the overarching quest. It’s an effective way to build a mysterious world, but it can be a bit overwhelming.

Gameplay:
The gameplay is polished and, for the most part, smooth. Yes, there are complaints about the difficulty, particularly with regard to boss design, damage sponges, and certain balancing issues like power creep and tight timing windows. However, the game also offers a diverse arsenal of tools, strategies, and approaches to overcome challenges. I never felt boxed in, and I loved the freedom it gave me to experiment with different playstyles.
The open-world design is another point of contention for some, but personally, I found it to be a breath of fresh air. As a fan of open-world games who has grown weary of the often formulaic design in recent titles, Elden Ring reinvigorated my love for exploration. The world feels vast, mysterious, and rewarding to discover, with a sense of scale and wonder that kept me hooked for hours. The roleplaying aspect was another highlight—getting lost in this world and shaping my own experience was immensely satisfying.

Final Thoughts:
Overall, Elden Ring is not perfect, but it's undoubtedly one of the best games I’ve ever played. Dark Souls 1 and Elden Ring have solidified my love for FromSoftware's games. I’ve always admired their design philosophy, their intricate lore, and their bold artistic choices. Despite its flaws, I’m happy to give Elden Ring a solid 9/10. It’s a game that will stay with me for a long time.

Another amazing title by FromSoftware, though not without its flaws.
Combat is significantly richer than the Dark Souls series, with greater build variety, weapon skills, and an extensive magic system.
The world design is the best it has ever been. The open-world design is not ideal for such a game since you can become over-leveled in certain areas; however, considering the late game is relatively linear, this is not a big issue.
The game is not particularly difficult if you are a veteran of the Soulslike genre. Most main story bosses are incredibly well-designed and feel fair to fight.
The biggest issue, however, is the quality of many field and dungeon bosses, most of whom are uninspired and feel like a chore to beat. This becomes especially annoying when you fight the same copy-pasted boss in different flavors ten times.
My other complaint is the length of the game. This game does not have enough story to support the 100-hour gameplay requirement.

Despite the considerable frustration one may experience during the few over-difficult boss encounters, Elden Ring is easily one of the best examples of open-world storytelling, world-building, and epic scope in all of gaming history. The suffering ultimately rewarding.

Elden Ring does a "show, don't tell" approach to its narrative and historical lore, relying on environmental storytelling rather than direct exposition. The world is meticulously crafted, with a consistent history and lore woven into every corner of the game. This encourages players to uncover the story through exploration, rather than through excessive cutscenes or expository dialogue. 

The open-world design of Elden Ring is the ideal open world experience, as compared to the more formulaic structure of Ubisoft-style games. Rather than focusing on completing a checklist of map markers, fetch quests, or trivial objectives, Elden Ring encourages exploration through a desire to unlock boss fights, and advance the story, and players continually move to the new. Motivation comes from a genuine curiosity about the world’s history and lore, which are gradually revealed through discoveries. The game avoids all-too-common retroactive continuity errors or incoherent storytelling issues that are so common in modern games. While it occasionally flirts with "moon logic" (puzzles or progression that might feel a bit too obscure), the overall narrative structure is cohesive and engaging.

Where do I even start... First things first - this game is an absolute masterpiece and easily one of the best games I’ve ever played. FromSoftware really outdid themselves, taking everything that made their previous games so special and bringing it into a massive open world, spicing it up with mechanics like horse combat along the way.

The sheer amount of lore, details, hints and connections scattered throughout the world is mind-blowing. Piecing together fragments of history, character lore and references to the previous Miyazaki's creations is a game in itself. This is a long-standing feature - you may like it or not but it adds to the sense of exploring the world, and I think it's a good thing.

Speaking of the world, it’s beautiful. The landscapes are very varied and interesting to ride around, from the sprawling fields to the poison swamps (of course), stunning castles. One can complain that there's too many variants of the poison swamps in this game and it's absolutely true. But I consider it a minor nitpick.

The gameplay and bosses are exactly what you’d expect from FromSoftware — great, recognizable and slightly upgraded again. Combat feels really good and impactful. I gotta say that I've had the most fun fighting the humanoid bosses in particular. As always, it's just way more comfortable to watch their moves and learn them. They feel more tactical and responsive, which turns some duels into straight up dances once you get the flow and learn how to counter. The variety of weapons, magic, and items brings a lot of variety to the build possibilities, giving you the freedom to often try something new. Unfortunately, armor upgrade system didn't make a return so armors have less of an impact compared to items, spells and weapons.

Of course, Elden Ring isn’t without flaws. Some bosses get reused a bit too often - Ulcerated Tree Spirit, Erdtree Avatar and Burial Watchdog are probably the worst offenders. It gets a bit tiresome fighting them again and again, especially when sometimes they aren't even changed, just stacked into a duo or released as regular enemies. And the questlines… man, they can be super convoluted. I appreciate the "figure it out yourself" approach from the previous Souls games, but with a world this big, it just collapses without a proper quest journal or a better guidance. It’s so easy to lose track of who said what and where they went, and it left me missing the more guided structure of the older Dark Souls games. In retrospect, those games feel tighter, and I appreciate them even more now. Elden Ring just rambles a lot because of the open world, it's both its blessing and somewhat of a curse.

Camera is a long-standing issue and I can't say it's improved in any way here. Why can't it zoom out during fights with large creature bosses? Why can't we still lock onto legs? Sometimes it's frustrating to the level of catching yourself at the thought that the camera ss working against you.

But despite these nitpicks, I had an absolute blast with Elden Ring. I spent over 200 hours exploring, fighting, reading and getting lost in the Lands Between, and I don’t regret a second of it. It’s truly one of the best games I’ve ever played, and even with its imperfections, it stands as a monumental achievement in gaming, to be remembered and compared to for generations to come.

This is all coming from someone who's not a heavy Soulsborne player, who was convinced to hop into this game by a good friend. So, bearing that in mind, here's what I've gotta say about good ol' Elden Ring.

It's fantastic.

There are few games whose combat systems feel so good and so rewarding to someone like me. I've got some deeply-rooted anger issues, so you'd think this game would be a pretty major turn-off considering how persistent you have to be against all of the different bosses of this game. And yet, despite all of the attempts I've poured into all of these bosses, the rush of adrenaline I feel after finally laying one out after hours (and sometimes days) of attempts far surpasses the frustration of the attempts. That right there is what keeps me coming back. Sure, the aforementioned combat system may be a bit harsh to the newer Soulsborne players, but it's soooooooooooooo satisfying when you get it down. Especially when you dodge straight through an attack that would one-shot you otherwise (and probably has one-shot you multiple times already).

None of that combat praise even touches on the weapons/buildcrafting of this game. There are a good deal of different ways to play the game. Wanna enact your greatest wizardry fantasies and hurl a buncha blue space magic at everything? You can do that. Wanna find a way to knock off as big of a chunk of a boss's health bar as possible? You got it. Wanna put on your best M1 Abrams tank cosplay and take little to no damage from any boss in the game? Go right for it. Getting to explore each and every one of these different builds has been a treat, and there is a great deal more to experience. In regards to weaponry, FromSoftware did an impeccable job with making each and every weapon look and feel so unique. Each weapon has its own niche, can be built into in some way, and has the aesthetics to match. That's not even mentioning the joy and wonder one feels when coming across a fresh new armament that they have the chance to experiment with. That diversity is pretty hard to nail down consistently, but FromSoftware have hit the nail on the head.

That all being said, the game got off to a bit of a confusing start for me. The central objective of this whole game was a bit ambiguous from the get-go, as was the central story. However, after having now beaten the game three different times, it feels as if that ambiguity was purposeful. That lack of a hard-set objective promotes exploration at the player's own pace. And with a world that is as expansive and detailed as the Lands Between, it's really easy to get lost in that exploration, both physically and metaphorically. As you explore, you not only uncover more of the secrets of this game's environment, but you also have the chance to learn more about the story of the Tarnished, and how they fit into the overall story of Elden Ring. And trust me when I say that there are a LOT of minute story and environment details that can very easily be missed. Even as I'm about to play the game a fourth time over, I know that there are still elements of the game that I have yet to experience. That trait gives much and more to the replay-ability of this game. This game's world is so vast and so filled with lore that hitting every possible point in one single run of the game seems a daunting task, to say the least. I can't imagine that it's impossible, but I also can't imagine it being a simple trot through the Lands Between. However, I'm not going to let that stop me from at least making an attempt.

TL;DR: I adore this game and the diversity it carries throughout its environment, weapons/combat, and story. The way they set up the capacity for each of these elements to be explored was perfect for the type of game these people have created. This game is a work of art and a fantastic gateway into the world of the Soulsborne games. I cannot recommend it enough.

It's open world Dark Souls - it's everything fromsoft fan boys have been dreaming about since DS3. The world is beautiful yet horrifying, bosses range from eldritch horrors to your new waifu, and if you start panic rolling then you know you're about to die.

Of the souls games, this is definitely the most approachable. It's certainly not easy, but if you find a boss that is consistently whooping your ass, you can just go somewhere else and fight something easier, or go search for new cool items/armor/weapons, or explore a completely new area just to see a different color palette. The catch to this is that it's very easy to overlook an area and when you come back to it you're now over-leveled. Maybe that's a good thing for you (makes a hard game easier), or maybe that's a bad thing for you (undermines the challenge).

My only real complaint about the game is the replay-ability does not feel the same as previous souls games. The first play through is such a special and wonderful experience of discovery and piecing together the dystopian lore of the Lands Between. But when it comes to NG+ or starting a fresh play through, it can feel like a slog; it's very easy to run around the huge map to find your favorite weapon/talismans and get a solid build set up within 1-2 hours of gameplay, but like... that running around and just collecting stuff is not what makes these games so fun and special. (I complain about this, but I have beat the game fully once, and have at least 4 other characters started with different builds and am still having a ton of fun)

The DLC (Shadow of the Erdtree) kicks ass. It's just more Elden Ring and it's absolutely HUGE for a DLC in terms of new bosses, areas to to explore, and new weapons/items/etc. My only complaint is the upgrade system with Scadutree Fragments (they give you a flat percentage increase to your damage and damage resistance. IMO, the Scadutree Fragments in conjunction with traditional leveling up system requires too much mental math to gauge if you're appropriately leveled up/prepared for a given area/boss in the DLC. If you're brand new the souls genre, I would say you don't need to buy the DLC until you've played enough of the base game to feel like you're hooked on the experience.

After I got [url=https://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198122670762/recommended/570940/]coerced[/url] into playing Darksouls 1 some years ago, I've finally taken the plunge and gave Elden Ring a try as well. I've been trying to avoid Elden Ring content for the last 2 years, so I managed to do my playthrough mostly blind.

[h3]The good[/h3]
[list]
[*]It's basically everything good about Darksouls, but more. 
[*]The combat system (waiting for openings, attacking, dodging, parrying, countering) feels good after getting used to and practicing it a bit.
[*]Big improvement of quality of life. The amount of Sites of Grace as save points is generous, travel through areas via horse is swift, switching between locations is easy via fast travel. Upgrade material can be bought after finding the correct items. The location of NPCs you found is marked on the map
[*]It's a big world with many enemies and many bosses. Besides the main areas, there are many small dungeons to find.
[*]More factions, more item descriptions, more lore.
[/list]

[h3]The bad[/h3]
[list]
[*]The game feels a bit treadmill-y. Upgrading your weapon is important to keep up with the general powercurve of enemies, but if you unexpectedly leave the area containing the specific level of upgrade materials your weapon requires, you're in for a tough time.
[*]I've only played Dark Souls 1, which taught me to expect traps and ambushes at every corner. While there are certainly many such things in Elden Ring, I'd say the size of the game works against it in this regard. There are secrets and shortcuts (especially in dungeons), but many areas feel 'stretched out', almost empty in comparison.
[*]I've managed to find my way through the game blind and many of its systems and secrets are explained somewhere, but in total, I feel like I missed a great many things. While this proboably encourages multiple playthroughs to engage with events/NPCs differently, I mostly found myself exhausted towards the end of my playthrough, as I couldn't be sure if I ever understood like half of the events that I experienced.
[/list]

Overall, I definitely recommend this game on the basis of its visual presentation and combat mechanics alone. Now excuse me as I'm going to put it aside and spend the next few weeks wiki-diving and watching VaatiVidya videos in attempt to understand it all.

The open world was interesting. The areas looked amazing and felt very distinct, especially in the DLC. The exploration felt very rewarding in most areas. Some of the later areas felt more linear with less rewards for exploration, but that wasn't too bad. One part that was really annoying though is that you can't open your map in combat for some reason even though you can open your inventory in combat, so if you're going somewhere and accidentally aggro something, you have to wait for the enemy to leave before you can check your map. Another thing is that there are some areas that are very easy to miss because they're optional and kind of hidden. The downside to that is that those areas have some of the best bosses so you could accidentally skip those.

The graphics, art design, and music are all phenomenal. The Bayle run-up was one of the coolest things I've seen in a game.

My biggest gripe with this game was the story/side quests. If you've played the Dark Souls games, Elden Ring follows a similar system of story and lore delivery. Most of the background for the story is in item descriptions and a lot of the dialogue is kind of vague. I think that works well in Dark Souls as the games are relatively short, but with an 80+ hour long game, I personally would have preferred if there was a bit more of a concrete delivery to drive the game. One thing though is that this might be a bit my fault for my play through. You have an NPC companion with you most of the game who tells you things about the game when you rest at Sites of Grace. About halfway in, I made a story decision that pissed my companion off so she told me she was gonna kill me and then she left, so I was confused as fuck for the rest of the game. Anyways, I feel like the side quests had a similar issue. With a lot of them, it's very confusing to tell what to do next. There's no in game quest tracker so most of the quests require guides. A good amount of the quests involve back tracking to areas you would never go to a second time, going to hidden areas, or doing things like repeating the same action multiple times for seemingly no reason. I honestly didn't even know I was on some quests. Sometimes people would just say random shit and apparently that was them asking you to do things. Sometimes NPCs would just be like "I must leave now forever" and I would think that was the end of the quest, but apparently it was like the halfway point in the quest. I think that works well in the dark souls games because you can replay them pretty quickly, but in a long game, it's just kind of annoying.

There were also a few mechanics that felt a bit under-baked. The game has a crafting system for making consumables. Throughout the game, you pick up a lot of flowers and random materials for crafting and you can turn those into bombs, arrows, healing items, and things like that. The downside is that most of the items are kind of mid so there isn't too much use in making them. To be fully honest, I kept forgetting crafting was an option. Upgrading weapons was also kind of weird. You need to get these smiting stones to upgrade weapons. You can either buy them or collect them in the world. The problem is that they don't tell you how many you need to fully upgrade a weapon so in the late game, if you pick up an item and want to get it to max level, you have to either lookup online what you need and buy it, or run back and forth between the blacksmith and the dude who sells the smiting stones. Also, you don't know what stats a weapon is going to have at full level so you can't compare new weapons to fully upgraded weapons without upgrading it. I also think the scadutree fragment and spirit ash system in the DLC could have benefited from an in game tracker so you know what you're missing.
Good game.
